title: N-Queens & Board Backtracking
summary: Placing N non-attacking queens via backtracking, tracking column and diagonal conflicts in O(1) per placement instead of rescanning the board.

slides.markdown:
N-Queens asks for every way to place N queens on an N×N board so that no two attack each other — no shared row, column, or diagonal. It's a [backtracking framework](backtracking-framework) problem over a board instead of an array, and it's the canonical example of why **conflict tracking, not board rescanning**, is what separates a working solution from one that times out.

The structural trick that makes this tractable: placing exactly one queen per row means the search never has to consider row conflicts at all — it only ever needs to check columns and diagonals against queens already placed in *earlier* rows, which shrinks what would otherwise be an O(N²) placement problem into an O(N) row-by-row decision.

Since no two queens can share a row anyway, the search is structured to place exactly one queen in each row, row by row from top to bottom. At row `r`, the only decision is **which column** to place the queen in — and that decision only needs to be checked against queens placed in rows `0` through `r-1`, since no later row exists yet to conflict with.

This is the same shape as [combinations](combinations-combination-sum)'s forward-only index, applied to rows instead of array positions: once row `r` is settled, the search never revisits it, so the state to check against only ever grows in one direction and never needs to be rechecked from scratch.

```python
def solve_n_queens(n):
    solutions = []
    cols_used = set()

    def backtrack(row, placement):
        if row == n:
            solutions.append(placement[:])
            return
        for col in range(n):
            if is_safe(row, col, cols_used):   # column + diagonal check
                cols_used.add(col)
                placement.append(col)
                backtrack(row + 1, placement)
                placement.pop()
                cols_used.remove(col)

    backtrack(0, [])
    return solutions
```

The base case is `row == n` — every row has a queen, so `placement` is one complete, valid board. `is_safe` is doing the real work here and is the entire subject of the next few slides: naively, it rescans everything placed so far; the fast version tracks conflicts directly.

Maintain three sets across the whole search: `cols_used` (columns with a queen), `diag1_used` (one diagonal direction), `diag2_used` (the other diagonal direction). Checking whether `(row, col)` is safe becomes three O(1) set lookups — no loop over previously placed queens at all.

Adding a queen at `(row, col)` adds `col` to `cols_used` and the two diagonal keys (below) to their sets; removing it during backtracking removes the same three entries. This turns what would otherwise be an O(row) check per placement — rescanning every earlier queen — into O(1), which matters a great deal given how many placements the search attempts overall.

slides.sectionTitle: Why row−col and row+col identify a diagonal
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: an N×N board (N=5) with two diagonals highlighted in different colors — one running top-left to bottom-right, with every cell on it annotated with its row−col value (all equal, e.g. 0), and one running top-right to bottom-left, with every cell annotated with its row+col value (all equal, e.g. 4) >>>

Every cell on the same top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal shares an identical `row − col` value (moving one step down-right increments both row and col by 1, leaving the difference unchanged). Every cell on the same top-right-to-bottom-left diagonal shares an identical `row + col` value (moving down-left increments row and decrements col, leaving the sum unchanged). So two integers — `row − col` and `row + col` — uniquely identify which of each diagonal family a cell belongs to, which is exactly what `diag1_used` and `diag2_used` key on.

slides.sectionTitle: Rescanning the board on every placement
Pruning a row the moment every column is blocked
slides.markdown:
If every column in the current row conflicts with `cols_used`, `diag1_used`, or `diag2_used`, the inner `for col in range(n)` loop simply finds no safe column and the row's backtracking function returns without ever placing a queen — that failure automatically propagates back up to the row above, which then tries its next column.

No special-case code is needed for "this row is fully blocked" — it falls out naturally from the loop finding zero safe options and the function returning without appending anything. This is the same implicit-pruning behavior seen in [subsets](subsets-power-set) and [combinations](combinations-combination-sum): a branch dies simply because nothing inside it satisfies the safety check, not because of an explicit early-exit condition written specifically for that case.

slides.sectionTitle: Counting solutions vs. returning the first one
slides.markdown:
| | Count all solutions | Return the first valid solution |
|---|---|---|
| What changes in `backtrack` | Increment a counter at `row == n`, keep exploring all branches | Return `True` immediately at `row == n`, and every caller returns `True` up the stack without trying further columns |
| Search space explored | Entire tree, every valid leaf found | Stops the instant one leaf is found — could be a tiny fraction of the tree |
| Typical use case | "How many ways to place N queens" | "Is a solution possible at all" or "give me any one valid board" |

The backtracking skeleton is identical; the only change is whether success at a leaf triggers "keep searching" or "stop everything and propagate true." Getting this wrong in either direction is a real bug: forgetting to keep exploring when counting silently undercounts, and forgetting to short-circuit when only one answer is needed wastes the entire remaining search for no benefit.

slides.sectionTitle: The pruned search tree for N=4
slides.markdown:
<<< Image: search tree for N=4 N-Queens, 4 levels deep (one per row) — root branches into 4 column choices for row 0; most second-level branches are drawn crossed-out immediately (column or diagonal conflict with row 0's queen); the two surviving branches continue to rows 2 and 3, with one reaching a valid 4-queen placement at the bottom and being marked as a solution leaf, the other dying at row 3 with no safe column left >>>

Of the 4^4 = 256 raw column combinations across 4 rows, the vast majority die within the first one or two rows purely from column and diagonal conflicts with the row-0 queen — only 2 of the 256 combinations survive as valid solutions for N=4, and the conflict-tracking prune is what keeps the search from wastefully exploring most of that dead space.

slides.sectionTitle: Why solution count outpaces N despite pruning
slides.markdown:
The number of distinct N-Queens solutions grows roughly exponentially with N — 2 for N=4, 10 for N=5, 92 for N=8, over 14,000 for N=12 — even though the O(1) conflict tracking keeps each individual placement cheap. Pruning shrinks the *search tree* dramatically relative to the raw N^N possibilities, but it can't shrink the *output* below however many valid boards genuinely exist, the same asymptotic floor seen with subsets (2^n) and combination sum (no closed form, but still output-bound).

The practical consequence: N-Queens is comfortably solvable up to roughly N=15-20 with good pruning (column and diagonal sets), but grows infeasible well before N=30, not because the pruning is weak, but because the solution count itself is genuinely enormous by then — no amount of algorithmic cleverness changes how many valid boards there are to enumerate.
